newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa attempts damage control on East Timor.
newsitem.headline: South Africa attempts damage control on East Timor.

text.p: South Africa, trying to unravel twin diplomatic blunders in its East Timor peace initiative, on Tuesday acknowledged a "miscommunication" over an announced visit by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters a misunderstanding had led him and other government officials to announce that Annan would meet President Nelson Mandela in Pretoria on Friday to discuss a joint initiative for peace in Indonesian-controlled East Timor.
"There was a miscommunication with the United Nations and I must say the miscommunication appears to have been largely on our side," he told Reuters.
South African officials also acknowledged on Tuesday that the Portuguese government had lodged a formal protest against the expulsion last week of its ambassador in Pretoria, Vasco Valente.

Although there was no formal response from the South African government early on Tuesday, Foreign Ministry officials said they were aware that South African Ambassador Kingsley Makubela had been summoned to the Portuguese Foreign Office.
The Portuguese embassy in Pretoria confirmed on Monday that Valente last week was given 48 hours to leave the country.
South African government sources said Valente was ordered out after details of a personal letter from Mandela to Indonesia's President Suharto were leaked to the Portuguese press.
Mandela wrote to Suharto in mid-July asking him to free jailed East Timorese rebel leader Xanana Gusmao as a first step towards peace in the territory.
In a bungle not yet explained by South Africa, Mandela's letter was delivered to the Portuguese embassy and not to the Indonesian mission.
It was neither returned nor forwarded.
Mandela became involved in the issue last month when he visited Suharto in Jakarta and met Gusmao.
He has since pledged his support for U.N. efforts to secure peace in East Timor and resolve the dispute over the territory's government.
Mankahlana said Annan had asked for an opportunity to visit Mandela and discuss the East Timor conflict, but not as at first thought in the immediate future.
South Africa now expected a visit from U.N. special representative Jamsheed Marker, who is heading talks in New York between Portugal and Indonesia, he said.
Mandela came under fire several years ago for accepting a huge donation to his now ruling African National Congress from Suharto without condemning his human rights record.
